title: US Proposes Ending Deference on H-1B Extensions, Raising Scrutiny for Indian Workers
excerpt: DHS wants to delete the rule that makes USCIS defer to prior approvals on Form I-129 extensions. The proposal, published October 14 with comments due November 13, would force employers to prove eligibility afresh — and it lands alongside a final rule ending automatic work-permit extensions.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed removing 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), the rule that tells USCIS officers to defer to a prior approval when an employer files an extension involving the same worker and the same facts.
  • The proposed rule was published in the Federal Register on October 14, 2026 (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529); public comments close on November 13, 2026, and the change is not yet in effect.
  • DHS estimates about 208,429 extension petitions a year benefited from deference and projects roughly 6,044 additional requests for evidence annually if the rule is removed.
  • What this means for you: if your employer will file an H-1B or L-1 extension, prepare the petition as if it were a first filing — full evidence of the job, your qualifications and the worksite — because a prior approval may no longer carry weight.

The Trump administration has proposed ending the policy under which U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services officers give deference to a previous approval when deciding whether to extend a foreign worker's visa petition. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published the proposed rule, titled "Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility," in the Federal Register on October 14, according to IANS and The American Bazaar. It would delete the regulation at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), which was only written into the regulations in December 2024, in the final weeks of the Biden administration.

Under the current rule, when an employer files Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, to extend a worker's stay or petition and the parties and underlying facts are unchanged, the USCIS officer starts from the earlier favourable determination. The officer can depart from it only where there was a material error, a material change, or new material information that hurts eligibility. The proposal would remove that instruction. Officers could still consider a prior approval, but they would no longer be required to begin from it, and each extension would be decided on the evidence in front of them.

Why DHS wants the change

DHS argues that the statute places the burden of proving eligibility for every immigration benefit on the petitioner, applicant or beneficiary, and that deference distorts that allocation. In the department's words, "the deference regulation and policy effectively shift the burden from the petitioner to the USCIS officer to justify departing from a prior approval." The department also says the policy risks "potentially perpetuating erroneous prior approvals and creating an environment in which fraudulent and meritless petitions are less likely to be detected."

"The deference regulation and policy effectively shift the burden from the petitioner to the USCIS officer to justify departing from a prior approval."

— U.S. Department of Homeland Security, proposed rule

DHS cited USCIS site-visit data: for H-1B extensions in fiscal 2022-2025, when deference applied, the combined non-compliance and fraud rate at visited sites was 22.39 per cent, against 16.77 per cent in fiscal 2018-2020 under the no-deference policy. For L-1A extensions the figures were 24.46 per cent against 18.37 per cent.

A policy that has swung for two decades

Deference has been reversed repeatedly: USCIS issued it as guidance in 2004, withdrew it in October 2017 during Trump's first term, restored it in April 2021 under President Joe Biden, and codified it in December 2024. This proposal would amend the regulation itself, making the change harder for a future administration to undo by memo. The provision covers more than H-1B — Form I-129 extensions include L-1, O-1, E-3 and TN workers — but Indians will feel it most: they account for the bulk of H-1B holders, roughly 70 per cent of beneficiaries, and a large share of H-4 spouses, according to IANS.

A second, final rule on work permits

The proposal arrived alongside a separate final rule ending automatic extensions of employment authorisation documents. Previously, a timely EAD renewal kept a work permit valid for up to 540 days while it was pending; that bridge is now gone. Commenters warned that H-4 processing times "frequently exceed the recommended filing time of 180 days" and predicted "unavoidable work gaps." DHS acknowledged dependents "may experience temporary lapses in employment authorisation," and estimates 20,000 to 33,000 EADs could lapse in an 18-month window starting in May 2027, at a cost of $138.1 million in lost employer productivity and $312.1 million in labour turnover.

What happens next

The deference change is a proposal, not law. The existing regulation remains in force while DHS takes comments through November 13, 2026, after which the department must review submissions before issuing any final rule. Employers and immigration lawyers expect more requests for evidence, longer adjudications and less predictable renewals if the rule is finalised. For now, workers approaching an extension face no change in the rules that govern their current petition — but they should expect the next one to be argued from the evidence, not from the last approval.
